messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case vignette accurately reflects a specific cognitive model.

CRITICAL: The two lists below are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE and OPPOSITE in meaning.
- REQUIRED edges MUST appear in the vignette. Finding them is a GOOD thing — do NOT flag them as violations.
- FORBIDDEN edges must NOT appear. Finding them IS a violation.
- An edge that is in REQUIRED is by definition NOT in FORBIDDEN, even if it looks similar.
- Always check the exact direction (A→B ≠ B→A) before classifying an edge.

STEP 1 — ACTIVE COMPONENTS
Every component below must appear clearly in the vignette.
Active components:   - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers
Inactive components (must NOT appear at all):   (none)

STEP 2 — REQUIRED EDGES (must be present)
Each of these causal connections must appear explicitly or be clearly implied.
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
→ FAIL only if a required edge is completely absent from the vignette.

STEP 3 — FORBIDDEN EDGES (must be absent)
These causal connections must NOT appear — not explicitly, not implicitly.
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

What counts as an implicit violation:
- A and B described together in a way that implies one causes the other
- One component immediately follows another, implying causation
- The narrative "cycle" passes through a forbidden link
→ FAIL if any forbidden edge appears. When genuinely uncertain about a forbidden edge, FAIL.

STEP 4 — VERDICT
Before returning your verdict, confirm:
- You have NOT flagged any edge from the REQUIRED list as a violation.
- Every flagged violation comes from the FORBIDDEN list.

Return a JSON object with two fields:
- "verdict": exactly "PASS" or "FAIL"
- "reasoning": 1-2 sentences naming the specific edge(s) that caused a FAIL, or confirming all required edges are present for a PASS

Vignette:
She is a 23-year-old Israeli student who has been struggling since a sexual assault that left her with a persistent sense that the world is unsafe. In day-to-day life, she describes being especially unsettled by cold air, by being touched without warning, and by crowded places, all of which can quickly make her feel as though she is back in danger. In those moments, her body reacts before she can think clearly: her heart pounds, breathing becomes difficult, and she feels intensely watchful, as if she must scan constantly for anyone who might harm her. Nights are also difficult, with trouble falling asleep or staying asleep adding to the exhaustion she already carries through the day.

Her memory of the assault is not organized into a coherent story; she says she cannot seem to put it into words, and when she remembers it, it feels as if it is happening right now. The event returns to her in a repetitive, film-like way, intruding into ordinary moments and making her feel trapped in the same frightening scene. These memory experiences are tightly linked to the situations that unsettle her most, and they also feed her sense of immediate threat, deepening her hypervigilance and physical distress. She has come to expect danger in ways that shape her view of others, holding the conviction that one can never know who will harm them.

To manage this ongoing fear, she keeps her mind occupied almost all the time and stays alert for dangerous people. She often stays up until very late, partly to avoid settling into sleep, and she describes herself as drawn into situations that remind her of the assault, including being in the dark. She also seeks out conversation with others about what happened and what followed, while at the same time putting her body under stress in ways that seem to leave her even more activated. These coping efforts appear to be her way of living with the constant sense of danger and the intrusions that accompany it.

Over time, these patterns have taken a toll on her studies, rest, and relationships. She feels that if she thinks about the event, she will not be able to handle it, and she also carries a painful belief that somebody else would have stopped it from happening. The overall picture is of a young woman whose world has narrowed around fear, alertness, and exhaustion, with her daily life increasingly organized around avoiding overwhelm while still remaining braced for threat.
